paragraphs.source_en: I shall leave the bath-tub side at that, and turn my gaze to the washing hall in the bathhouse. There they were, in great numbers indeed: a whole crowd of Adams, some squatting and some sitting, scrubbing various parts of their bodies in every imaginable posture. Of these, the two Adams who most astonished me were one lying on his back on the cement floor, gazing up at the high skylight; the other lay face down, peering into the drain; this was an Adam of considerable leisure. There was also a monk squatting toward the wall, while behind him a little monk kept beating his shoulders. This was probably a matter of master and disciple, the disciple performing the bath-attendant's duties in his stead. There was a proper bath attendant too. He seemed to have caught cold, for even in this heat he wore a sleeveless jacket and poured hot water from an oval pail over the bathers' shoulders. Between the big toe and its neighbor on his right foot he had wedged a small piece of coarse flannel for rubbing off bodily grime. Over here a man greedily hugged three little pails to himself and kept saying to the person beside him, “Please use my soap.” Then he went on talking endlessly about something or other. When I listened closely, what he was saying turned out to be: “Guns came over from foreign countries, you know. In the old days everyone fought with broadswords; foreigners were cowards, and that is why they invented guns. This foreign country does not seem to have been China; at any rate it was foreign, and in Watonai's time there were no guns yet. Watonai, after all, was of the Seiwa Genji line. They say that when Minamoto no Yoshitsune crossed from Ezo to Manchuria, a very learned Ezo man went along with him. Later Yoshitsune's son attacked the Great Ming; the Ming, being in trouble, sent an envoy to the third shogun to ask for three thousand troops, and the third shogun detained the fellow and would not let him return. What was that envoy called again? Some kind of envoy, anyhow. So they kept that envoy there for two whole years, and in the end, at Nagasaki, they gave him a courtesan; the child born to that courtesan was Watonai. After that, when he went back to his country, he found that the Great Ming had already been destroyed by traitors...” I could not make the least sense of what this gentleman was talking about. Behind this man was a gloomy-looking fellow of twenty-five or twenty-six, silently and repeatedly fomenting the root of his thigh with hot water; he seemed to have a boil or something there, and looked as though it pained him badly. Beside him was a seventeen- or eighteen-year-old, talking away in a rough, affected tone; he was probably one of the local “students.” Next to this “student” was a man with his back turned this way; each joint of his spine stuck out distinctly, as if a bamboo-jointed staff had been thrust into a corpse, and on both sides of the spine four moxibustion marks were neatly arranged like pieces set out on a board for Sixteen Soldiers. Some of those “Sixteen Soldiers” pieces were inflamed and ulcerated, and some even had pus around them. If I go on writing in this fashion, there will be far too much to write; with my skill I could not manage to describe even a tenth of it. I was beginning to regret having started such a troublesome undertaking.

paragraphs.source_zh: 浴池方面就叙述到这里，我把视线移向了浴室当中的大厅。嚄，多着哪，多着哪，一大群亚当们或蹲或坐，以种种不同的姿势正在搓洗身体的各个部位，其中最使我吃惊的是两位亚当，一位仰身躺在水泥地上，瞧着高高的天窗；另一位朝下趴着，往水沟里瞧着，这是位悠闲的亚当。还有一个和尚面向墙壁蹲着，身后一个小和尚不断给他敲打着两肩。这大概是师傅和徒弟的关系，徒弟在代行搓澡的工作吧。也有正式搓澡的，看来他可能是在患感冒，室内这么热，却还穿着一件坎肩，用椭圆小桶往浴客肩上浇热水。在他的右脚的大拇指中夹着一小块用来搓身上油垢的粗绒布。在这边有一个人贪婪地抱着三个小水桶，不断向他旁边的人说：“请用我的肥皂。”然后没完没了地讲着什么。我仔细一听，原来他讲的是：“枪是外国传来的，是吧。古时候都是抡大刀的，外国人没胆量，所以才造出枪来。这个外国好像不是中国，反正是外国，和唐内时还没有呢。和唐内也就是清和源氏嘛。听说源义经从虾夷到满洲去的时候，一个很有学问的虾夷人跟着去了。后来源义经的儿子去攻打大明国，大明国方面受不了，于是派遣一个使者来见三代将军，提出要借三千兵马，三代将军把那个家伙留下来不放他回去。这个使者叫什么来着？好像是个叫什么的使者。这样把这个使者一直扣留了两年，后来在长崎给了他一个妓女，那个妓女生的孩子就是和唐内嘛。以后他回国一看，大明已经被国贼消灭啦……”这位老兄说的都是些什么，我一点也听不懂。在这人身后有个二十五六岁满脸晦气的家伙，闷声不响地不断用热水在热敷他的大腿根部，似乎那地方生了疮，显出很疼的样子。在他的旁边有个十七八岁的人，语气粗野，不断哇啦哇啦讲着什么，他大概是这一带“书生”一流的人吧。在这个“书生”的旁边有个人背朝向这边，他那脊椎骨的关节一一凸起，活像一具僵尸被插进一根竹节杖，而且在他脊椎两侧整齐地各排列着四个炙点，活像“十六子棋”棋盘上排列的四个棋子儿。他的这些“十六子棋”的棋子儿还有些溃烂，有的还出现脓水。这样写下去，可就要写得太多了，以我的本领想写出它的十分之一也无法胜任。我正在后悔不该搞起这件麻烦事来。

paragraphs.source_en: Just then, at the entrance, there suddenly appeared a bald-headed man of over seventy, dressed in pale yellow cotton. Bowing respectfully to these naked monsters, he said, “Heh-heh, thank you all, as always, for your kind patronage. It is rather cold today, so please take your time bathing. If you go in and out of the medicinal bath several times, you will warm yourselves nicely. Hey! Bathhouse keeper! Mind it carefully, and be sure to keep the bathwater hot enough.” He poured out this long speech without a pause. The bathhouse attendant answered, “All right.” The fellow who had been holding forth about Watonai praised him: “That old man has real charm. You cannot run a business unless you are like that.” Having suddenly encountered this curious old man, I was rather startled, so I shall leave my description of that side as it stands and devote myself for a while to observing him. The old man first noticed a boy of about four who had just come out of the bath, held out his hand, and said, “Young master, come over here!” The child, frightened at the sight of this wretched old fellow, burst out crying with a loud “Waa!” The old man seemed somewhat disappointed and exclaimed, “What, are you crying? What is it? Afraid of this old man? Well, well!” Unable to do anything else, he immediately shifted his tack and addressed the child's father: “Ah, good day, Gen. It is a bit chilly today. That thief who broke into Omiya last night, what an absolute fool he must have been. He cut a square hole in the little door; isn't that ridiculous? Then he ran off without stealing a thing. I suppose a policeman or a night watchman must have come along.” After loudly ridiculing the thief, he turned to someone else and said, “Yes, yes, cold today, is it not? You are young, so perhaps you do not feel it much?” In truth, it was only the old man himself who was so thoroughly afraid of the cold.
